cells.tense: You are reading what each thing in front of you actually needs, and you act on that without overruling it.
cells.ask: Pick one plant or one person, give it the next small thing it needs today, and stop there.
cells.core:
You see what's in front of you — what's reaching, what's tired, what's just slow — and you act on it without overruling it. A seedling gets to be small. When you say what someone's growth needs, it tends to be right, and you don't spend that on force.

Knowing and care are pointed the same direction here. You can hold several readings of a thing at once and still give one clear next move. The meal gets made, the hard thing gets said plainly, the person gets to be where they are. Stay in the bed — patience that stops showing up turns into distance, and being present with the thing is what keeps the read alive.

cells.tense: You are already tending the version of this that hasn't arrived, and you are building for it now.
cells.ask: Take one thing you're tending, name what it needs this week, do only that, and write nothing down about next month.
cells.core:
You're out ahead of what's actually here. The reading runs past the shoot in front of you — plans for a yield that isn't seeded, corrections to something that hasn't gone wrong, support built before the plant can use it. What moves you is genuine, which is exactly why it's hard to see, but it's pointed at something that doesn't exist yet, so the things that are here feel handled rather than tended.

What eases it isn't caring less. Let this week's growth be this week's size. Give one result the room to be whatever it turns out to be, not what you've already settled it will be. What you see is good. It just needs something real in front of it.

cells.tense: You can still see what the bed needs, and you no longer say it out loud to anyone.
cells.ask: Say one thing you've noticed about someone near you, plainly and without softening it, and let their reply stand as it is.
cells.core:
Here's how it looks when this is working: you notice what's thirsty, what's crowded, what's ready, and you say so — one clear thing, to the person it's about, and then you let them do what they do with it. Reading the bed and speaking what you read are the same motion. What you notice is useful to the people in it, not just to the plants.

The hands keep working — water, spacing, the quiet adjustments — and none of it leaves your mouth. Let someone else's read of the same thing meet yours, not to settle who's right, just to touch. A bigger garden won't help. Being in the same soil as the people in it will.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what grows around you, and you describe it as things simply turning out that way.
cells.ask: Pick one recent choice you made about what someone else grows and say, out loud, that it was your call.
cells.core:
Here's how it looks when this is working: you know what you decided and you can say it — this is what got watered, this is what got left alone, this is what was meant to grow. The choices still get made, and they carry your name. The people near you can see the shape of your hand in what surrounds them.

What's happening now is the same choosing without the name on it. What you water, what you leave dry, what you say nothing about — it adds up, and the people near you are growing under it. When it comes up, you call it the obvious thing, or what anyone would do, or not really a choice at all. Say one line as yours and the whole arrangement gets simpler to live in.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person does this alone, so the cells avoid 'you alone' and instead name the discipline of tending as the arena. The reader could say 'I talk to plenty of people, I just don't bring this' — the ask still lands, because it is an act of saying, not a claim about their social life. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any version of 'you're not making it safe enough for them,' which reads the other person's experience through the person's fault; I cut that. The ask survives being wrong: if the capacity is not what I think, saying one unfinished thing aloud still teaches them where the work is.
